presentingComplaint: Progressive breathlessness and wheeze over 2 days in a frail elderly woman with long-standing asthma.
history: 78-year-old lifelong non-smoker, frail (uses a walking frame, lives with daughter), with asthma since her thirties maintained on low-dose inhaled corticosteroid/long-acting beta-agonist. Over the past 2 days she has had increasing breathlessness, an audible wheeze and a dry night-time cough that wakes her, following a coryzal illness in her grandchild. She has needed her salbutamol inhaler every 2-3 hours with only partial, transient relief. No chest pain, no orthopnoea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, no ankle swelling, no fever or purulent sputum. Comorbidities: hypertension, type 2 diabetes, osteoporosis. She has had two similar episodes over the past year, each responding to oral steroids. Poor inhaler technique noted at last review; she often forgets her preventer. No recent travel or immobility.
examination: Frail, alert, speaking in short phrases but able to complete sentences with effort. Using accessory muscles, mild intercostal recession. Widespread bilateral polyphonic expiratory wheeze with prolonged expiratory phase; air entry reduced but symmetrical, no focal crepitations, no bronchial breathing. JVP not raised, no peripheral oedema, heart sounds normal with no added sounds or murmur. Calves soft and non-tender. Peak expiratory flow 150 L/min (personal best 320 L/min, ~47% predicted). No cyanosis.
imaging: Chest radiograph: hyperinflated lung fields, no consolidation, no pleural effusion, no pneumothorax; cardiac silhouette normal, no upper-lobe diversion or interstitial oedema.
microbiology: Not indicated; no fever or purulent sputum. Respiratory viral swab pending (index coryzal contact).
finalDiagnosis: Acute asthma exacerbation (moderate-to-severe, viral-triggered) in a frail elderly woman with long-standing atopic asthma
citations: GINA - Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention - 2024
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Asthma
stewardship: Non-infective exacerbation; no antibiotics indicated. Reserve antibiotics only if clear evidence of bacterial infection (fever, purulent sputum, radiographic consolidation).
contraindications: Caution with sedatives given hypercapnia risk in fatigue
Monitor serum potassium with repeated beta-agonist nebulisation
Systemic steroids will raise blood glucose in this diabetic patient - monitor and adjust
edgeCases: Silent chest or rising PaCO2 signalling life-threatening asthma and need for critical-care review
Elderly wheeze frequently mislabelled as heart failure or COPD - normal BNP, normal cardiac silhouette and lifelong non-smoker with childhood-onset reversible disease point to asthma
Frailty and accessory-muscle use may mask fatigue; monitor for exhaustion
expectedMaiK: Recognise a moderate-to-severe acute asthma exacerbation and treat promptly with controlled oxygen to target SpO2 94-98%, repeated inhaled short-acting beta-agonist plus ipratropium, and early systemic corticosteroids, while excluding heart failure and PE as mimics.
expectedNextQuestions: What is the personal-best/predicted peak expiratory flow and current percentage?
Is she able to speak in full sentences, and are there signs of exhaustion or a silent chest?
Any orthopnoea, PND or leg swelling to suggest cardiac cause?
Inhaler adherence and technique, and number of exacerbations/steroid courses in the past year?
Any fever, purulent sputum or pleuritic pain suggesting infection?
expectedInvestigations: Pulse oximetry and arterial blood gas if deteriorating or SpO2 <92%
regressionAssertions: Must recommend inhaled short-acting beta-agonist and systemic corticosteroid
Heart failure and COPD must appear only as differentials, not as the final diagnosis
Oxygen target 94-98% should be used, not high-flow uncontrolled oxygen
